title: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) in Nigeria: a family’s starting guide
excerpt: A practical starting guide to spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) for Nigerian families: understand the diagnosis, organise records and prepare your next care questions.
summary: SMA causes muscle weakness and can affect breathing and swallowing.
A specialist assessment and genetic testing help establish the diagnosis.
Ask what needs attention now, who will arrange it and whom you can contact.

sections.title: What is spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)?
paragraphs: Spinal muscular atrophy, usually shortened to SMA, is a genetic condition that causes muscle weakness. It can affect children and adults. Some people need help with sitting or moving around; others also need support with breathing or swallowing. The needs of one person may be very different from those of another.

SMA affects motor neurons, the nerve cells that carry signals to muscles. In the common SMN1-related form, the body does not have enough of a protein these cells need, called survival motor neuron protein. You may hear it shortened to SMN. Understanding this can help when medical terms start appearing in appointments and reports.

A child does not develop SMA because a parent failed to exercise them. It is not an infection they caught from another child. Nor does needing physical help tell you what someone understands, enjoys or hopes to do. When discussing care, include the person with SMA whenever they can take part.

sections.title: SMN1, SMN2 and SMA type labels
paragraphs: SMN1 and SMN2 are gene names. The common form of SMA involves changes in SMN1. Doctors may also discuss the number of SMN2 copies, because this can influence the condition. A copy count alone cannot tell you exactly what will happen to a particular child or adult.

You may also hear “5q SMA” or a type number, such as type 1, 2 or 3. Type labels have traditionally described when symptoms began and which movement milestones a person reached. They can help a doctor describe the condition, but people with the same type can still have different needs. Treatment can also change the picture.

When a type number comes up, ask: “What does this mean for us now? What needs checking, and what support might help?” Keep the genetic result, the person’s current abilities and their care needs in view. The report cannot tell you everything about breathing, swallowing or how someone manages at home and school.

sections.title: Questions to ask when medical language is unfamiliar
paragraphs: You may hear an unfamiliar term, nod, and realise later that you are not sure what it meant. Ask the doctor to write it down and explain it again. You can say, “What does that mean in everyday language?” or “What do we need to do about it this week?”

If a test is being arranged, ask what it is looking for and who will explain the result. Keep a copy of the complete report. If you would prefer the conversation in another language, ask about an interpreter. You can also bring someone you trust to take notes, if that would help.

sections.title: What can you do before a specialist appointment?
paragraphs: Write a short account of what you have noticed: when the concern began, what has changed and any previous appointments or tests. Bring the actual reports, including results you were told were normal. A specialist may need to see what was tested rather than rely on the word “normal”.

Before travelling, call the clinic to check that it sees patients in the right age group, whether you need a referral and how to book. Ask which records to send ahead, if any. Confirming an appointment is useful, but the booking office may not be able to tell you what testing or treatment the doctor will recommend.

sections.title: Medical records to keep after an SMA diagnosis
paragraphs: Keep reports together in a folder, with current instructions and appointment details easy to find. A secure digital copy can be useful too, if you can make one. Share medical documents only when there is a reason to do so, and check who will receive them before sending them to a group chat.

sections.title: Seeking SMA care in Nigeria
paragraphs: The Federal Ministry of Health’s teaching-hospital directory can help you find institutions to contact. Call the hospital through an official number and ask about paediatric neurology for a child, or adult neurology for an adult. Check the clinic day, booking process and referral requirements before making the journey.

You could begin with: “We need an assessment for a child with suspected SMA. Which department should we contact, and what should we bring?” If the diagnosis is confirmed, say so. Ask whether the service can review the test report and what happens after that review. A listing for neurology does not tell you whether SMA testing or a particular treatment is available there.

source.title: Federal Ministry of Health: teaching hospitals

sections.title: Your next step after a suspected or confirmed diagnosis
paragraphs: If you are waiting for a diagnosis, arrange the assessment and gather the reports you already have. If SMA has been confirmed, ask which needs require attention first and who to contact about the next appointment. You do not have to arrive knowing which specialist does what.

Explain the practical difficulties too. If the journey involves another state, if you cannot afford a proposed test, or if you need help caring for other children while you travel, tell the team. These things affect whether you can carry out the plan. Ask what can be arranged around them.

sections.title: Build a first-week plan that the household can use
paragraphs: After an appointment, the jobs can pile up quickly: collect a report, call another clinic, arrange transport, find out the cost of a test. Write them down and agree who can help with each. Keep unanswered medical questions for the care team rather than asking relatives to fill in the gaps.

A relative may be able to book transport or collect a prescription without needing the whole medical history. Another may help with meals or school runs. Give people the information they need for the job they have agreed to do, and keep full reports available for the professionals who need them.

If an instruction is beyond what you can currently manage, say so. Ask the team what to do while you work through the barrier. That might mean discussing travel, equipment or a follow-up visit. You should not have to quietly abandon a recommendation because you are embarrassed to explain the cost.

The arrangements will need attention again when circumstances change. A new school term, a move or losing someone who usually helps with transport can upset a routine that was working. Let the care team know when a change affects care, and ask supporters for help with the specific gap.

intro: If you have just heard the words spinal muscular atrophy, you may be trying to understand the diagnosis while also working out where to find help in Nigeria. You might have a test result in your hand, a referral to arrange, or questions you did not think to ask until you got home.

SMA is a genetic condition that causes muscle weakness. Here we explain the terms you are likely to hear, how to prepare for an appointment and what to ask before travelling for care. You do not have to learn everything at once.

faqs.question: Is SMA the same as muscular dystrophy?
faqs.answer: No. SMA and muscular dystrophies are different conditions. Similar muscle weakness does not establish the diagnosis; a clinician decides which assessment and tests are appropriate.

faqs.question: Can SMA affect adults as well as children?
faqs.answer: Yes. SMA can present at different ages. Adult symptoms also need clinical assessment, particularly when an earlier diagnosis is uncertain.

faqs.question: Where should a Nigerian family start?
faqs.answer: Start with a qualified clinician who can assess the concern and arrange an appropriate neurology referral. Confirm the receiving clinic’s service and booking requirements before travelling. The foundation can help you organise questions, but does not diagnose SMA.

faqs.question: Does an SMA type predict exactly what will happen?
faqs.answer: No. A type label is a clinical description, not a precise forecast for an individual. Current function, treatment and the person’s care plan matter.

faqs.question: Can I contact SMA Hope before all my records are ready?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use Support or the contact page for a practical conversation. You do not need to publish your child’s laboratory report in a public group to ask for help.

title: After an SMA diagnosis: an appointment checklist for families
excerpt: Prepare for an appointment after an SMA diagnosis: prioritise questions, gather reports, discuss travel and costs, and leave with clear follow-up actions.
summary: Bring your full reports and the questions you most want answered.
Write down who is arranging each referral and how to follow it up.
Tell the team about costs, travel or other difficulties with carrying out the plan.

sections.title: Questions to ask after an SMA diagnosis
paragraphs: Before the next visit, write down the three questions you most want answered. They may be simple ones: “What does the result mean?”, “What needs to happen first?” and “Who do we call if our child becomes unwell?” Show the doctor your list near the start, so the questions do not get lost in everything else.

Leave room underneath each question for the answer. If an unfamiliar term comes up, ask what it means before moving on. You can return to longer-term questions at another visit; for now, make sure you understand anything you are being asked to do before you leave.

sections.title: Reports to bring to an SMA appointment
paragraphs: Bring the full laboratory report, referral letters and hospital discharge summaries. A short timeline can help: when the concerns began, what changed and where you have already been seen. Include the current medicines list, allergies and equipment in use. If a report is missing, note the hospital, department and approximate date, and ask how to obtain a copy.

If you already have a video that shows a movement concern, ask whether the doctor would find it useful. Do not put off seeking care to make one. Describe what you have seen in ordinary words; you do not need to identify the muscle or nerve involved.

You can bring someone you trust to listen or take notes. Agree beforehand how you would like them to help. If the person with SMA can take part, ask what they want to discuss and give them time to speak. Bring prescriptions or labelled packaging if requested, rather than trying to reconstruct medicine instructions from memory.

sections.title: How the SMA care team should coordinate
paragraphs: You may be referred to several professionals. Neurology, breathing care, rehabilitation and nutrition can each be part of SMA care, alongside other support. Ask what each referral is for, which appointment comes first and who is keeping track of the overall plan.

Sometimes advice from one service affects another: a seating change may need input from therapists and school staff, for example. Ask how the professionals share information. If two instructions seem to conflict, ask them to clarify. You should not have to decide on your own which instruction to follow.

source.title: SMA Europe: standards of care and the multidisciplinary team

sections.title: Planning travel, clinic visits and costs in Nigeria
paragraphs: Tell the clinic if you are travelling from another state, depending on a relative for transport or taking unpaid time off work. Ask whether any appointments can be arranged on the same day, and whether any are too urgent to wait. Check where each referral goes; booking a visit in one department may not book the next one.

Before paying, ask what the charge includes. Is the quote for a consultation alone, or does it include a test and a visit to discuss the result? If you are using insurance or an employer scheme, check what approval is needed first. Keep written quotes and record whom you spoke to if an answer was given by phone.

sections.title: Agree the next actions and follow-up contacts
paragraphs: Near the end of the visit, read back what you have written: “We will book this test, your team will send that referral, and we should call this number if we have not heard by Friday. Have I understood?” It is easier to clear up a misunderstanding while you are still in the room.

For every result or referral, ask who will follow it up. Does the clinic call you, or do you need another appointment? If someone says, “We will be in touch,” ask when to expect contact and whom to call if you hear nothing. Keep the number with your appointment notes.

sections.title: Share the care plan with the right people
paragraphs: Once you are home, decide who needs which information. Someone collecting a report needs to know where to go and what permission is required. Someone picking up a sibling from school needs the time and address. They do not all need the genetic report.

It may help to keep full clinical documents in one folder and a shorter list of household jobs elsewhere. Put a name beside each agreed task. If nobody can take on a job, you can see the gap and ask for help. Keep unclear medical instructions on a separate question list to take back to the team.

sections.title: What if the next referral is delayed?
paragraphs: Start by asking whether the receiving service has the referral. If it does, ask whether anything is missing and when you should check again. Write down the date and department you contacted. If you cannot get an answer, return to the referring clinic and explain what happened.

Ask the care team how long it is appropriate to wait and what changes need earlier attention. A missing letter and a medical decision to monitor something are different problems. Serious breathing difficulty, choking or sudden serious illness needs emergency care; do not wait for a routine appointment or a reply through the foundation’s chat.

Keep copies of the referral and your enquiries so you can show the next person what has already happened. If another appointment is suggested, tell the team about bookings you already have. That can help avoid paying twice for the same assessment or leaving different services unaware of each other.

There is also the rest of family life to manage. Someone still has to work, make meals and look after siblings while you follow up the referral. Ask a supporter for a task they can take off your list this week. Getting through the paperwork does not mean you have finished coming to terms with the diagnosis.

intro: An SMA diagnosis can leave you with questions long after the appointment has ended. What happens next? Who do we call? How will we pay for this? You may remember the name of a test but little of what was said around it.

For the next visit, bring the full test report and write down the questions you most want answered. The checklist and table below will help you keep track of the answers, referrals and costs without having to hold everything in your head.

faqs.question: What should I bring to an SMA appointment?
faqs.answer: Bring the full test report, referral letters, relevant clinic summaries, the current medicines list and your three most important questions. Ask the clinic in advance whether it needs other documents.

faqs.question: Should another family member come with me?
faqs.answer: If you want that support, a trusted person can take notes or help with travel. Agree their role beforehand and involve the person with SMA in the discussion wherever possible.

faqs.question: What if I cannot afford the proposed plan?
faqs.answer: Explain the constraint before leaving. Ask the care team to discuss priorities, possible alternatives and any verified support routes. Do not independently change prescribed care to fit a budget.

faqs.question: Can I send a laboratory report to the foundation on WhatsApp?
faqs.answer: Begin with a general question and ask which information is needed and how it should be shared. Avoid sending identifiable health documents until an appropriate private route and purpose are agreed.

faqs.question: Does the checklist replace the clinician’s care plan?
faqs.answer: No. It organises questions and follow-up. Diagnosis, treatment and urgent-care instructions come from the treating team.

title: SMA care costs in Nigeria: a practical family budget
excerpt: Plan SMA care costs in Nigeria with a family budget covering appointments, travel, supplies, equipment maintenance and dated quotations.
summary: Separate one-off purchases from recurring expenses.
Request written quotes and verify what each includes.

sections.title: What belongs in an SMA care budget?
paragraphs: A headline treatment price can be so large that everything else gets overlooked. Start with what you need to pay for this month. List the item, what it is for, the estimated cost, when payment is due and who is arranging it. If you do not know the amount, write “quote needed” and come back to it.

Keep purchases separate from regular expenses. A device may be a one-off payment, but parts, supplies and journeys can keep coming. Also separate money you have received from money someone has offered. Even a generous promise from a close relative may not be available on the day a bill is due.

sections.title: Care expenses beyond the clinic bill
paragraphs: A consultation may also involve transport, an overnight stay, meals, childcare for siblings, or time away from paid work. If a relative provides transport at no charge, note that contribution separately so the plan still makes sense if they are unavailable next time.

Suppose the clinic has quoted for a consultation. You still need to get there, perhaps stay overnight and arrange for someone to collect another child from school. Put those costs on the same page. If a relative offers to drive, note that too, along with whom you could ask if they become unavailable. The journey still needs arranging even when it costs you nothing.

sections.title: Equipment purchase, power and maintenance costs
paragraphs: Before buying clinician-recommended equipment, ask who will fit it, teach you to use it, service it, and supply compatible parts. Where equipment requires electricity, discuss power and backup arrangements with the supplier and care team. A cheaper purchase may not be cheaper over its useful life if servicing is unavailable.

For an imported item, ask the supplier for a written breakdown of shipping, customs-related charges, installation, warranty coverage, and expected delivery. Ask which currency the quote uses and when the price expires. Do not assume a foreign-currency price will remain unchanged in naira.

Ask for the exact model and the parts it uses to be named on the quote. Check who you call if it breaks and whether the warranty can be used in Nigeria. Would a repair mean sending it abroad? Arrange the training and follow-up your care team recommends before buying. Those services may not be included in the delivery price.

sections.title: How to compare SMA care quotations
paragraphs: Put the quotes side by side and check what you are actually buying: the exact item or service, delivery time, fitting, support, payment terms and refunds. First confirm with the clinician that it is suitable. Then compare prices for the same thing. A supplier can explain a product, but cannot replace the clinical advice behind the purchase.

For insurance or employer benefits, ask the scheme directly about the specific test or service, any authorisation needed, and reimbursement evidence. Keep the answer in writing where possible. A general statement that a scheme covers hospital care does not establish coverage for every SMA-related expense.

Compare quotations on the same basis. One laboratory may include specimen collection and result discussion, while another lists only the analysis. One equipment supplier may include fitting and local servicing, while another includes neither. Mark differences explicitly instead of putting only two headline amounts side by side. Ask each provider to confirm the missing items before deciding that a package is more affordable.

sections.title: Organising financial and practical support
paragraphs: Instead of asking one person to solve the whole budget, identify a defined need: a booked journey, a quoted test, a week of meals, or an agreed contribution to a recurring expense. Offer a way to help without demanding access to private medical details. If you fundraise publicly, agree who can share the story and which documents must stay private.

Keep a simple ledger of funds received and expenses paid. Store receipts securely. Explain any change in the intended use of donations to supporters. This protects relationships as well as the family’s recordkeeping.

For a regular expense, ask whether the offer is a one-off payment or a monthly contribution. Agree when to check in again. If several people are helping, choose someone the family trusts to keep the record. You can update supporters about money received and spent without sending them private medical reports each time.

sections.title: Reviewing a care budget with the family
paragraphs: Choose a time each month to go through what has been paid and what is coming next. If there is not enough money, explain the gap to the care team and ask about priorities and alternatives. Do not stop prescribed care to make the figures balance. Remember the costs of looking after siblings and giving caregivers time to rest too.

sections.title: A budget template you can use
paragraphs: The table below is a template, not a list of Nigerian tariffs. Put each supplier or clinic quote beside its date and scope. Use “awaiting quote” for anything you have not confirmed. If a quote is in another currency, keep the original amount and record the exchange rate used for planning.

For a treatment programme, ask which assessments, medicine, administration, monitoring, travel and follow-up costs are included. A low headline price may describe only one part. Do not interpret a manufacturer’s foreign-market list price as the amount a Nigerian family will necessarily pay.

At the monthly check, look at four things: bills paid, bills due, quotes that need renewing and needs that have changed. Keep the original currency beside a naira estimate so you can update it. If you put aside extra money for unexpected costs, label it as your own allowance. Replace estimates with actual prices as you get them.

sections.title: How can the foundation help with cost questions?
paragraphs: If you are unsure what to ask a clinic or supplier, contact SMA Hope through Support. We can help you put the questions in order. The provider still needs to confirm the service, price and payment details directly; a conversation with us does not mean an application has been accepted.

If you are considering the book in Nigeria, contact us for an availability and delivery enquiry. The foundation is working out a local supply route; a confirmed book price should include the chosen edition and delivery arrangements. A book purchase and a donation are separate transactions.

Sometimes the missing detail is small but expensive: a delivery charge, an unnamed laboratory or an expired quote. Ask about it before paying. Keep receipts and financial records somewhere secure, and agree who can see them. People helping with money should respect the family’s decisions and privacy.

intro: How much does SMA care cost in Nigeria? There is no single figure that will tell you what your family will spend. The answer depends on the care needed, where you can get it and how often you need to travel. The price of a medicine is only part of the bill.

Begin with the expenses you already know, then ask for written quotes for the next tests, appointments or equipment. This guide walks through what to include, what to ask a provider and how to compare quotes without overlooking recurring costs.

faqs.question: How much does SMA treatment cost in Nigeria?
faqs.answer: There is no single price. Ask for a dated, itemised quote for the proposed care, including assessment, medicine, administration and follow-up. Add travel and other household expenses separately so you can see what the family would actually need to pay.

faqs.question: Are the test prices in this guide a Nigerian SMA tariff?
faqs.answer: No. The dated public example is a broader hereditary-conditions panel that includes SMN1, not an independently verified standalone SMA test tariff. Ask for the exact test, method, current price and inclusions before using any figure.

faqs.question: Should I budget in naira or a foreign currency?
faqs.answer: Keep a Nigerian household budget in the currency you use, but retain the original currency of each imported or overseas quote. Record the planning conversion separately and recheck it before committing.

faqs.question: Can insurance or an employer scheme pay?
faqs.answer: Ask the scheme about the exact service, authorisation requirements and exclusions. General hospital coverage does not establish coverage for a particular genetic test or SMA treatment.

faqs.question: Does buying the book pay for a family’s treatment?
faqs.answer: Buying the book and making a donation are separate. If you want to contribute towards treatment or another specific need, ask the foundation whether there is a current fund for that purpose and how the money will be used.

title: SMA genetic testing in Nigeria: diagnosis and carrier tests
excerpt: Understand diagnostic and carrier testing for SMA, including test limitations and questions about laboratories, costs and results when testing from Nigeria.
summary: A diagnostic test and a carrier test answer different questions.
Ask which laboratory performs the test and who explains the result.
A negative result needs interpretation in the context of the test used.

sections.title: Which SMA genetic test is being requested?
paragraphs: A clinician may recommend testing to investigate suspected SMA, or a relative may ask about being a carrier. These are different purposes. Before paying for a test, ask the referring clinician to write the exact test and the question it is intended to answer. A general health screening package or routine blood count is not the same thing as an SMA genetic test.

“Genetic testing” can mean several things. One test may count copies of a gene; another may look for particular changes or read its sequence. Ask your doctor why they have chosen this analysis and what happens if the result does not explain the symptoms. A larger panel is not always the test that will answer the question.

sections.title: Diagnostic testing versus SMA carrier testing
paragraphs: Diagnostic testing investigates whether genetic findings explain the person’s symptoms. Carrier testing looks for a genetic change that a person may pass on without having the condition themselves. For the common SMN1-related form of SMA, genetic counselling helps families understand inheritance, test limitations, and reproductive options. Some carrier configurations can be missed by standard copy-number testing, so a negative carrier result does not remove all risk.

For the common autosomal recessive form, when both parents are carriers, each pregnancy has a one-in-four chance of a child being affected. Each pregnancy is a separate event; the outcome of a previous pregnancy does not use up or reset that probability. A genetics professional should relate this general explanation to the actual family results, including any uncertainty about the variants or the testing method.

sections.title: Can a negative SMA carrier test miss a carrier?
paragraphs: Yes. Some people have two SMN1 copies on one chromosome and none on the other, often described as a 2+0 or silent-carrier configuration. A copy-number result alone may not distinguish that arrangement from one copy on each chromosome. Interpretation depends on the method, additional markers and family context.

Detection and residual-risk estimates can differ between ancestry groups. A negative screen must therefore be interpreted using the laboratory’s validated method and the individual’s family history, not a broad assumption that a test works equally well for everyone. Ask a genetics professional what the report means for you and whether further testing is appropriate.

This does not mean genetic testing is unreliable for everyone of African descent. African populations are diverse, and risk estimates from one study do not fit every family. Take earlier reports to the genetics appointment. Ask what those tests could detect, what they could miss and whether information from your family changes the interpretation.

source.title: Milligan et al.: interpreting silent-carrier results in SMA testing

sections.title: Questions about SMN1, SMN2 and a family’s report
paragraphs: Ask which genes and kinds of changes were examined. Did the analysis count SMN1 copies? Was SMN2 copy number assessed too? Does the doctor need sequencing or another analysis to answer the remaining question? You can ask these questions without being expected to interpret the answers alone.

A relative’s result may help clarify the family situation, but sharing it should be deliberate and private. Ask the genetics service which relatives’ results would be informative and how consent will be managed. Your clinician or genetics service can explain what the results say about your genes.

sections.title: Why might another analysis be needed after the first test?
paragraphs: Most people with the common form of SMA have a characteristic loss involving SMN1, but a smaller group have other relevant changes. A test designed for the common finding may therefore need to be followed by another analysis when the clinical picture and first result do not agree. The referring specialist decides whether further SMN1 analysis or investigation of a different condition is appropriate.

Before paying for a repeat test, ask what additional question it will answer and whether the original laboratory can clarify or extend its analysis. Repeating an identical test without a new clinical reason may not resolve the uncertainty. Keep the original report available, because the precise method and findings can guide that next decision.

sections.title: Arranging SMA genetic testing from Nigeria
paragraphs: In Nigeria, ask whether the specimen is processed locally or sent to another laboratory. Do not infer laboratory capability from an advertisement alone. Ask for the name of the laboratory doing the analysis, the method, what is included in the report, and how the referring clinician will receive it.
bullets: Is this the test requested by the clinician?
What sample is required, and who collects it?
Does the quoted price include transport, reporting, and an explanation of the result?
What happens if the specimen is unsuitable or delayed?
What is the expected turnaround time, and how will delays be communicated?

paragraphs: Before comparing prices, be clear about why the test is needed. A child with symptoms needs a diagnostic assessment. Parents asking about carrier status after a child’s diagnosis need advice that takes the child’s report into account. A pregnancy may bring different questions and deadlines. Tell the ordering doctor which situation applies.

Ask for the method in writing. Copy-number analysis, sequencing and an analysis of duplication-linked markers do not all provide the same information. A laboratory may use a combination, but a product title does not establish that combination. The ordering professional should explain why the proposed scope is appropriate and what would happen if the result remained inconclusive.

Two quotes may both say “SMA testing” and cover very different services. One might include collection and a screen; another might include the diagnostic analysis requested by your doctor and an appointment to explain it. Write down the test, laboratory doing the analysis and included services beside each price. Only then can you compare the amounts fairly.

sections.title: What should a cross-border testing quote include?
paragraphs: If a Nigerian specimen will be tested abroad, the laboratory doing the analysis and local ordering service should agree the specimen type, collection instructions, accepted paperwork, courier route and responsibility for a failed or delayed sample. Do not assume an ordinary parcel service is appropriate for a biological specimen.

Obtain the complete price and expected turnaround in writing, including whether collection, shipping, repeat sampling and an explanation of the result are included. CENTOGENE publishes international ordering and logistics information, but no SMA Hope partnership or Nigeria-specific price is confirmed by this page.

Ask who pays if a specimen cannot be analysed, whether a repeat collection is included and when the turnaround clock starts. It may start on receipt of an acceptable specimen rather than the day the family pays locally. Confirm whether the final report goes to the ordering clinician, the patient or both. Agree how a result requiring prompt attention will reach the responsible professional.

sections.title: How to review an SMA laboratory report
paragraphs: Ask for the full laboratory report rather than a screenshot of a single line. Check that the name and identifiers are correct. Keep the date, laboratory details, and ordering clinician’s information with it. If another hospital needs the report, share it through an agreed secure channel rather than posting it in an open support group.

Arrange an appointment to discuss the result. Ask what the finding confirms, what it does not establish, and whether any further testing is recommended. If a result appears inconsistent with earlier advice, request clarification from the clinician and laboratory rather than choosing one interpretation yourself.

Ask the person explaining the report to distinguish a finding from an estimate. “Two SMN1 copies detected” tells you what was counted. It does not settle every question about how those copies are arranged. “Reduced risk” also leaves some risk. Ask where the report explains that limit and whether your family history changes the advice.

sections.title: Genetic counselling and family decisions
paragraphs: A genetics conversation can involve parents, siblings, and future family plans. Decide who you want present. Ask for explanations that you can revisit after the appointment. These discussions should be confidential and free from blame; the purpose is to understand options and make informed decisions.

If testing is being considered for another family member, ask the genetics professional what is appropriate for that person and how consent should be handled. Avoid pressuring relatives to share private results publicly.

Counselling can cover whether other relatives might benefit from advice, what testing is available before or during a future pregnancy, and what the different choices can and cannot establish. It should leave room for the family’s values and the option to take time. A family member’s decision to seek information does not create an obligation for everyone else to test or to disclose reproductive plans.

sections.title: What happens after the SMA test result?
paragraphs: Put the result-review appointment on the calendar and record who will contact you. Ask what should happen while the report is pending. The family should not be left to coordinate every unanswered question by itself: request a clear contact point for clinical concerns and a separate contact for laboratory administration.

sections.title: What to write when asking about testing
paragraphs: “Our clinician has requested an SMA-related test for this purpose: [diagnosis, carrier assessment or another specified question]. Please confirm the exact analysis, laboratory doing the analysis and method, what the report includes, collection and shipping arrangements, the full quote and expected turnaround. Please also identify who explains the result and what happens if the specimen is unsuitable.”

Do not include a full medical history in an unsolicited first message. Ask which secure channel should receive the referral and reports. Once the clinician and laboratory agree the route, keep one record of the order, collection date, laboratory receipt and result appointment. This makes a delay easier to follow up without sending the same private documents to several unrelated contacts.

SMA Hope has not yet confirmed a laboratory partnership or a subsidised testing service in Nigeria. If we establish one, families will need clear information about the test, price, sample arrangements and who explains the result. For now, confirm each of those details with the ordering clinician and the laboratory.

checklist: Purpose and exact test confirmed with the clinician.
Performing laboratory, price, and turnaround clarified.
Consent and report-sharing arrangements understood.
Result-review appointment arranged.
intro: When someone says you need an “SMA test”, ask which test they mean. Testing a person who has symptoms is different from checking whether someone is a carrier. The report needs to answer the question you and your doctor are asking.

If you are arranging testing from Nigeria, find out which laboratory will analyse the sample, what its method can detect and who will explain the result. A negative carrier screen has limitations; the details of the report matter. Here is what to ask before paying or sending a sample.

faqs.question: Can I be an SMA carrier without symptoms?
faqs.answer: Yes. Carrier screening is intended to identify reproductive risk in people who may not have SMA themselves. Discuss your personal result and family history with a genetics professional.

faqs.question: Does a negative SMA carrier screen mean zero risk?
faqs.answer: No. Residual risk depends on the method and what it can detect. Ask the laboratory and genetics professional to interpret the actual report.

faqs.question: Is a routine blood count an SMA test?
faqs.answer: No. A routine blood count does not provide the same information as a specifically requested genetic test for SMA.

faqs.question: Can we send a sample from Nigeria to Germany?
faqs.answer: It may be possible, but your clinician and the receiving laboratory need to agree the arrangements first. Ask about sample collection, consent, packaging, shipping, price and the appointment to explain the result. SMA Hope does not currently offer a confirmed Nigeria-to-Germany testing service.

faqs.question: How much does SMA carrier testing cost?
faqs.answer: Request a current written quote for the named test and laboratory, with collection, shipping and interpretation stated separately. No Nigeria-wide tariff has been verified here.

bookContext: The meaning of a test result became a deeply personal question for our family. We tell that story in When Every Breath Matters. For questions about your own report, ask the clinician or genetics team who can review the test and your family history.

title: SMA treatment and access from Nigeria: what to verify
excerpt: Understand the questions to ask about SMA treatment evidence, eligibility, monitoring, costs and access when exploring care from Nigeria.
summary: A treatment’s existence does not establish local availability or individual eligibility.
Discuss both treatment options and ongoing care with a specialist.
Verify access arrangements directly before making payments or travel plans.

sections.title: Could this treatment help, and can we get it?
paragraphs: When you read about an SMA medicine, ask three questions: what does the evidence show, could it help this person, and how could they receive it? A news story may explain the research without answering the last two. Take the story to your specialist and ask which parts apply to your situation.

Tell the specialist what you hope treatment might change. Ask what benefits have been measured, how progress would be checked and what is still uncertain. A short video of another child cannot show their full medical history or all the care they received. It cannot tell you how your child will respond.

sections.title: SMA medicines: names and routes to discuss with a specialist
paragraphs: Nusinersen (Spinraza) and risdiplam (Evrysdi) are treatments that act on SMN2-related protein production; one is administered into the fluid around the spinal cord and the other is taken orally. Gene replacement therapies use a different approach. The specialist must explain which option, if any, is appropriate and what monitoring is required.

The medicines named here are examples, not a complete list. Ask the specialist for the exact product, how it is given and the current rules in the country where treatment is proposed. Those details, together with the person’s health, determine which options can be considered.

Ask what receiving the treatment would involve in practice. Where would you go? Is a procedure needed? Which tests and follow-up visits are required? An oral medicine still needs prescribing, a reliable supply and monitoring. A treatment given through a procedure needs a team equipped to provide it. Discuss the whole arrangement, including what it would ask of the family.

sections.title: How to verify treatment and access claims
paragraphs: Save the source and date of any claim you want to discuss. Distinguish a regulator’s approval, a clinical trial result, a manufacturer programme, and a family’s personal experience. They are not interchangeable. Ask the specialist which information applies to your circumstances and whether newer guidance changes the picture.

If someone advertises guaranteed access, ask for the named institution, written eligibility criteria, full costs, and official contact details. Verify the offer independently through the institution. Do not transfer money to a personal account on the strength of a forwarded message or a promise of a guaranteed outcome.

sections.title: What should an SMA treatment quote include?
paragraphs: Request an explanation that covers what happens before, during, and after treatment. A headline medicine price is not a complete care plan.

Ask for the quote to follow a timeline: assessment and investigations before treatment, medicine and administration, observation or admission if needed, then follow-up. Put travel and accommodation alongside the clinical costs. Confirm what happens if assessment finds that treatment should not proceed, including which costs have already been incurred and whether any deposit is refundable. Keep the written confirmation from the receiving clinical team and financial terms as separate written documents.
bullets: What assessment establishes suitability?
Which tests and monitoring are required?
Where would treatment take place, and who is responsible for follow-up?
What costs are excluded from the quoted package?
What happens if travel is delayed or eligibility changes?
Who manages a complication or an interruption in treatment?

sections.title: Planning SMA treatment outside Nigeria
paragraphs: Before booking travel, get written confirmation from the receiving clinical team about the appointment or proposed care. Ask about the expected stay, follow-up, payments, cancellations and care when you return. Discuss fitness to travel and transport with the treating team. Visa agents and fundraisers may help with arrangements, but medical decisions need the clinical team.

A programme that helped another family may have changed, closed, or used different eligibility rules. Date every access enquiry. Record whether the answer was confirmed directly, remains under review, or has not been verified.

Before travelling, ask who will look after the person when you return. Which records will the overseas team send, and which follow-up tests can be done locally? Contact the proposed Nigerian service to confirm that it can provide them. Agree how the two teams will communicate, rather than discover a gap after the trip.

sections.title: Supportive care while treatment is being explored
paragraphs: An access application can take attention away from immediate needs. Ask the team what support should continue while options are being explored. Coordinated SMA care can involve breathing, nutrition, movement, and wellbeing. Treatment decisions and supportive care belong in one individual plan.

Ask the local team what can be organised now for respiratory care, nutrition, rehabilitation, positioning and day-to-day participation. A medication search should not leave these needs without a plan. Families can ask for training and written instructions for the equipment actually prescribed to them, including whom to call about a fault. Internet instructions for someone else’s device or care routine are not a substitute for that training.

source.title: SMA Europe: standards of care and the multidisciplinary team

sections.title: US gene-therapy development: ITVISMA
paragraphs: The US FDA lists ITVISMA (onasemnogene abeparvovec-brve) for adults and children aged two years and older with a confirmed SMN1 mutation. This is a distinct product indication; do not assume it is the same formulation or eligibility pathway as Zolgensma. The current FDA product information should be discussed with the treating specialist.

sections.title: An additional US muscle-targeted treatment
paragraphs: The FDA approved ISEMBYLD (apitegromab-mstn) in September 2026 for people aged two years and older who are currently receiving an SMN2-targeted treatment. Its US prescribing information describes it as a myostatin-targeting antibody. This is an additional treatment category, not a reason to stop or change existing therapy without a specialist.

These are US approvals. They do not confirm Nigerian registration, supply or funding. If one of these medicines is relevant to a discussion with your specialist, use the linked FDA information and ask what access would involve for you.

sections.title: Questions to ask a treatment centre
paragraphs: Ask the proposed treating institution to identify the medicine and formulation, the clinician responsible, the written assessment process and the follow-up arrangements. An intermediary should not be the only source of confirmation. Use the institution’s independently verified contact route.

If the plan involves travel, establish what happens before departure, during treatment and on return. Obtain a written financial breakdown and ask what changes if the person is unwell or no longer meets the planned criteria. A visa, quotation or fundraising target is not written confirmation from the receiving clinical team.

Keep a short record of each answer, its date and who gave it. “The hospital has booked an assessment” means something different from “the hospital has accepted the person for treatment.” Likewise, an insurer receiving an application has not approved it. Being precise helps relatives and fundraisers understand what is still needed.

If you are asking several hospitals or programmes about care, show the replies to your specialist. They can help identify which options are relevant and which questions remain unanswered. This can save you paying for repeat assessments or pursuing a programme that does not cover the person’s diagnosis or age.

Verify provider and programme details through official channels.
Request a complete, dated cost and follow-up plan.
Agree ongoing care while access is being explored.
intro: Reading about an SMA treatment can bring hope and a difficult next question: can we get it in Nigeria? A medicine may be approved in another country while remaining hard to obtain or pay for here. It may also be unsuitable for a particular person.

The conversation with your specialist needs to cover the medicine itself, who can receive it, its benefits and risks, and the follow-up it requires. This guide explains those questions and the access issues to check. Where we discuss an approval in another country, that does not confirm supply or funding in Nigeria.

faqs.question: Is there a cure for SMA?
faqs.answer: Treatments can change the course of SMA, but should not be described as a guaranteed cure. Ask the specialist about realistic benefits, limitations and ongoing care for the individual.

faqs.question: Are SMA treatments available in Nigeria?
faqs.answer: This guide does not confirm local registration, supply or funding for a particular product. Ask the treating team and named provider to verify those points directly and in writing.

faqs.question: Does FDA approval mean I can receive the treatment in Nigeria?
faqs.answer: No. US approval is a US regulatory decision. Nigerian access, import arrangements, local care capability and individual suitability must be established separately.

faqs.question: Can a person combine or switch SMA treatments?
faqs.answer: That is an individual specialist decision governed by clinical evidence, product information and access rules. This guide does not recommend a combination or switching schedule.

faqs.question: What care is still needed while seeking treatment?
faqs.answer: Ask the care team about the individual’s breathing, nutrition, movement, equipment and wellbeing needs. An application for a medicine is not a substitute for an agreed daily care plan.

title: School support for children with SMA: an inclusion checklist
excerpt: Plan school support for a child with SMA: accessibility, classroom participation, privacy, responsibilities and a practical inclusion checklist.
summary: Start with the student’s goals and preferences.
Walk through a real school day to identify practical barriers.
Put responsibilities and review dates in writing.

sections.title: Ask the student what matters to them
paragraphs: Ask the student what they want from school. It may be a favourite lesson, seeing friends at break or joining a class activity. Their answer can reveal a difficulty adults have missed. Getting into the building matters, but so does being able to enjoy the day once inside.

Use those answers when planning attendance. A short visit may be worthwhile if the child can join an activity they love. A longer day may be exhausting if most of it is spent struggling between rooms. Agree what the child hopes to take part in, then discuss the time and support that would make it possible.

sections.title: Check school accessibility across the whole day
paragraphs: Arrange a visit that follows an ordinary school day: arrival, classroom, toilets, assembly, break, lunch, and departure. Check the route on a busy day if possible. A ramp at the gate does not solve an upstairs classroom or an inaccessible toilet.

Walk the route with staff while the school is busy if you can. Look for uneven ground, crowded corridors and furniture that blocks access. Check how the child would leave in an emergency. Ask who will sort out a problem on the day, especially if the usual entrance or room cannot be used.
bullets: Can the student reach and use their desk comfortably?
Is there enough space to move between rooms?
How will books, bags, and learning materials be carried?
What arrangements are needed for accessible toilets?
Where can the student rest privately if this is part of their agreed plan?
How will evacuation work, and who is responsible?

sections.title: Agree classroom support and independence
paragraphs: Ask what the student can and wants to do independently. Adults should offer help rather than automatically taking over. Teachers can discuss alternatives for activities that create barriers: changing the location, adapting materials, allowing a different way to respond, or planning suitable breaks. Any physical handling or medical care arrangements should follow professional advice and training.

In a Nigerian school, clarify transport, gate access, classroom allocation, and the practical roles of staff before term starts. If changes require spending, agree who is responsible and when they can realistically be completed. Avoid vague assurances that everything will be sorted after admission.

Keep the learning goal in view when changing how a task is done. If handwriting is tiring, could the student give the same answer another way? If someone helps them reach materials, can they still choose what to use? Offer the help needed without answering for the student. Ask again as their interests and classwork change.

sections.title: Write a one-page SMA school plan
paragraphs: Record the student’s preferences, agreed classroom adjustments, relevant contacts, and who will coordinate communication with the family. Medical instructions should come from the care team and be shared only with staff who need them. Decide how teachers will learn about changes without requiring the family to repeat their story to every new staff member.
Include a review date. A plan that worked last term may need adjustment when classrooms, timetables, staff, or equipment change. Ask the student what is working as well as what is difficult.

The one-page plan should point to any detailed care instructions agreed with the treating team, rather than attempt to replace them. Clarify which staff have been trained for the tasks they are expected to perform and who covers their absence. Decide how a parent will be contacted, what information a substitute teacher needs and where the current version of the plan is kept. Avoid relying on one staff member’s memory.

sections.title: Protect the student’s privacy and belonging
paragraphs: Agree how the condition will be explained to classmates, if the student and family want it discussed. Do not share medical reports or photographs in parent messaging groups without permission. Speak to the student directly and avoid presenting them as an object of pity. Include them in invitations, group work, and leadership opportunities.

If bullying or exclusion occurs, document the incident, raise it through the school’s safeguarding process, and ask what action and follow-up will take place. The family should have a named contact rather than an open-ended instruction to “let us know”.

Agree with the student and family what classmates will be told. A simple explanation of the help someone needs may be enough. Ask permission before using the child’s name, photograph or story in an assembly or fundraising appeal. They should also be included in the ordinary group work, invitations and leadership opportunities that make up school life.

sections.title: Plan schoolwork around appointments and illness
paragraphs: Ask how schoolwork will be shared if the student misses lessons for appointments or illness. Agree a manageable catch-up plan rather than automatically adding work to an already demanding week. Keep expectations ambitious but flexible, with the student involved in deciding what support helps.

sections.title: A school meeting agenda you can use
paragraphs: Ask for a meeting with someone able to agree practical arrangements. Bring the student’s priorities, the relevant care-team instructions and an access checklist. Walk the proposed route rather than relying on a statement that the school is “accessible”.

Record what will change, who will arrange it and when it will be checked. If the school cannot resolve a barrier immediately, ask what workable interim arrangement can be agreed. Review the plan when a classroom, timetable or staff member changes.

End the meeting with a few changes people can carry out. For example: clear the arrival route, agree another way to complete a classroom task and name the person who will tell the family about timetable changes. Put a person and date beside each job. Note any problem that remains unresolved so it is not forgotten.

rows: How will the student participate in class?
Can the student use classroom and toilets?
Which assistance is agreed and appropriately taught?
When will the student’s experience be checked?

sections.title: When a shorter school day is needed
paragraphs: Some students start with brief attendance or need a flexible pattern. Define what the time is for: a favourite lesson, a shared activity, meeting classmates or another agreed goal. A short visit should still include belonging and a chance to participate.

Ask how the child will stay connected when they miss school. This might include materials they can use, contact with classmates and a manageable return to lessons. The amount of attendance that suits one child should not become a rule for every child with SMA.

For a short attendance arrangement, choose a predictable activity with a clear beginning and end, then review how it works for the child. Keep home and school learning connected through an agreed task or update, without expecting parents to recreate an entire school day. Ask the student about friends and belonging, as well as fatigue and workload. The appropriate duration and care arrangements remain individual decisions with the family and relevant professionals.

checklist: Student’s goals and preferences recorded.
Arrival-to-departure access walk completed.
Named school contact and responsibilities agreed.
Privacy, emergency arrangements, and review date documented.
intro: For a child with SMA, a school day involves more than getting through the gate. Can they use the classroom and toilet comfortably? Join a lesson? Spend time with friends? Who helps when they need a break or physical support?

A school plan should answer those everyday questions with the child, their family and school staff. This guide looks at arrangements Nigerian schools can discuss, from getting around the building to agreeing who does what. The child’s own wishes belong in that conversation too.

faqs.question: Can a child with SMA attend school?
faqs.answer: Many children with SMA attend school with arrangements suited to their individual needs. The family, student, school and care team should plan participation and any support together.

faqs.question: Does a ramp make a school accessible?
faqs.answer: A ramp alone is not enough. Check classrooms, toilets, movement between activities, rest arrangements and evacuation responsibilities.

faqs.question: Who should know the child’s medical information?
faqs.answer: Share relevant instructions only with the staff who need them, through an agreed private route. Decide with the student and family what, if anything, to explain to classmates.

faqs.question: What if a full school day is not currently possible?
faqs.answer: Agree a realistic attendance and learning plan with the family, school and care team. Focus on meaningful participation and review the arrangement as needs change.

faqs.question: Should an untrained volunteer provide clinical care at school?
faqs.answer: No. Clinical procedures and physical handling require the appropriate agreement, professional instructions and training. A general offer to help does not establish competence.

bookContext: Teachers who want to understand more about family life with SMA may find When Every Breath Matters helpful. Tochukwu and Ijeoma Nkwocha write about their children and the care, relationships and hopes that surround a diagnosis.

title: How to support a family living with spinal muscular atrophy
excerpt: Practical ways to support a family living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA): reliable help, respectful visits, privacy and community support.
summary: Offer a task you can do at an agreed time, and leave room for a no.
Ask before visiting, sharing news, posting photos or organising an appeal.
Stay in touch about ordinary life as well as the diagnosis.

sections.title: Make a specific offer of help to an SMA family
paragraphs: “Let me know if you need anything” leaves the family with another job: working out what you might mean and asking for it. Try a specific offer instead. “I can take your other child to school on Tuesday and Thursday. Would that help?” gives someone a simple choice. Accept a no without asking them to justify it.

Choose something you can sustain. A reliable weekly contribution may be easier for a household to plan around than a large burst of help that disappears. Agree when you will arrive, what you will do, and how to contact each other if plans change.

Be honest about what you can keep doing. If a weekly commitment is too much, offer a single journey or one evening’s meal. Tell the family promptly if plans change. They may have arranged the rest of the day around your offer, so notice and a chance to find another helper matter.

sections.title: Practical ways to support SMA caregivers
paragraphs: Start by asking what would actually reduce pressure. Do not buy equipment or supplements because another family used them. Medical decisions and equipment suitability belong with the treating team.

There is plenty you can do without taking on medical care: shop, collect a prescription as agreed or spend time with a sibling. If the family needs help with a care routine, ask what training is required and who can provide it. Being willing to help is a good beginning; it is not the same as being ready to use equipment.
bullets: A planned school run or childcare for siblings.
Groceries chosen by the family, rather than unsolicited dietary advice.
Transport or help arranging an appointment journey.
A household task at a time that does not disrupt care.
Administrative help with organising receipts or appointment records, with permission.
Company, a phone call, or an ordinary shared activity.

sections.title: Respect care routines and family boundaries
paragraphs: Visits can be welcome and still require planning. Ask when to come, how long to stay, and whether the family has any visitor precautions. If you are unwell, tell them before visiting and follow their wishes. Avoid treating their boundaries as a personal rejection.

When help involves care tasks, do only what has been agreed and what you have been appropriately taught. Watching a caregiver once does not automatically make someone ready to take over. Ask what to do if a problem arises and who should be contacted.

Avoid making the family host you. Ask before bringing extra people, and do not expect a meal or a detailed medical update. If you are unsure what to do during a visit, ask. They may want conversation about something ordinary, a shared activity or simply company without having to explain anything.

sections.title: Faith and community support without pressure
paragraphs: Churches, mosques, and other communities can offer companionship, practical assistance, and a place of belonging. Ask the family what kind of support they welcome. Avoid blame, promises of a guaranteed cure, or pressure to stop treatment. A family should not have to defend its medical choices to remain part of a community.

If the family wants help from its community, ask whether one person could coordinate a small rota. That person can deal with routine questions and cancellations. Agree what can be shared with helpers so the family does not receive several calls about the same task or have its private information discussed at a meeting.

Ask before sharing a prayer request or discussing the family in a wider meeting. Let them choose how much to say. Avoid suggesting that illness reflects weak faith or that a particular outcome will prove someone believed enough. Faith may be a source of comfort; it should not become another burden the family has to manage.

sections.title: Permission for stories, photographs and fundraising
paragraphs: Consent to tell one friend is not consent to publish on social media. Explain exactly what you want to share, where it will appear, and who may see it. Give the family a chance to review the wording and images. A child’s dignity matters even when a fundraising appeal feels urgent.

Do not publish full laboratory reports, home routines, contact details, or identifiable documents to prove that a family deserves help. Ask what information can be shared and use the minimum necessary. If you are collecting funds, agree the purpose and how you will account for the money.

Before launching an appeal, agree who will approve the text, pictures and later updates. Decide where donations go and how spending will be recorded. You can explain what help is needed without publishing a child’s intimate care details. The family should be able to review the appeal before strangers see it.

sections.title: Stay connected with the whole family
paragraphs: Ask about school, work, friends and the things the family enjoys. Invite them to ordinary activities and let them tell you what arrangements would help. Include siblings without making them explain the diagnosis. A friendship should still have room for conversation that has nothing to do with illness.

sections.title: Organising help without adding more work
paragraphs: If the family wants a rota, begin with a short trial and one trusted coordinator. Agree a small set of tasks such as shopping, meals selected by the family, transport or administrative help. Put a named helper and backup beside each task.

The coordinator should deal with routine changes rather than asking the family to reorganise every cancellation. Keep clinical responsibilities outside the general rota. Permission to arrange a meal or visit does not authorise medication, feeding or equipment procedures.

Let the coordinator handle reminders, cancellations and finding another volunteer. Give helpers only the information they need. Check with the family how often they want an update. If the rota starts producing more messages and decisions than it saves, make it smaller.

Check the arrangement after a few weeks: which offers were useful, what went wrong and what has changed? Help that worked during an admission may be less useful once a child returns to school or a parent resumes work. Leave room for ordinary friendship. A family should be able to enjoy a conversation that is not a progress report on illness or fundraising.

sections.title: If you want to give the book to someone
paragraphs: When Every Breath Matters may help a relative or friend understand more about family life with SMA. Ask whether they would welcome the book, particularly if the subject touches a difficult experience of their own. For a group, the companion discussion guide offers questions to talk through after reading.

Use the official book page to choose the edition and Amazon store. For delivery in Nigeria, ask the foundation about current arrangements before sending payment. A thoughtful recommendation is more useful than pressuring a family to read or publicly endorse the book.

checklist: Make one specific offer you can reliably keep.
Agree timing, boundaries, and a contact person.
Ask permission for stories, photographs, and fundraising.
Check in again without demanding a medical update.
intro: “Let me know if you need anything” is usually kindly meant. But a parent managing appointments, work and care may not have the energy to turn that offer into a task. A specific offer is easier to answer: “Can I collect the shopping on Thursday?”
If someone close to you is living with SMA, you do not need to know every medical term to be helpful. Start by asking what would make this week easier. Then agree what you can do and follow through.

faqs.question: What can I say instead of “let me know if you need anything”?
faqs.answer: Offer something specific: a planned journey, groceries chosen by the family or a household task at an agreed time. Give the person room to say no.

faqs.question: Can I organise fundraising for the family?
faqs.answer: Ask permission first. Agree the purpose, wording, images, collection route and accounting. Do not publish health documents or identifiable information as proof without an appropriate agreed basis.

faqs.question: How can a faith community help?
faqs.answer: Offer belonging, companionship and practical assistance that the family welcomes. Avoid blame, guaranteed-cure claims or pressure about medical decisions.

faqs.question: Can I share their story to raise awareness?
faqs.answer: Obtain specific permission for what you will share, where and with whom. Permission for a private conversation does not automatically cover a public post.

faqs.question: Should I stop checking in if the family declines a visit?
faqs.answer: Respect the boundary and ask whether another form of contact would be welcome. A declined visit may reflect timing or care needs rather than the end of a friendship.

sections.title: Starting an SMA referral in Nigeria
paragraphs: If SMA is suspected or has been diagnosed, ask the current clinician which specialist assessment is needed next and how urgent it is. Request a referral letter that explains the concern, relevant findings, and tests already performed. A clear handover can reduce the need to retell the whole story at each visit.

If symptoms are still being investigated, begin with a doctor who can examine the person and advise on a referral. If SMA is confirmed, ask what the next service needs to know. Check whether it sees children or adults. A referral sent to the right department with the reports attached can save a long, fruitless journey.

sections.title: Confirm specialist services before travelling
paragraphs: The Federal Ministry of Health’s teaching-hospital directory can help you find hospitals to contact. Call through an official number and ask which department handles your enquiry. Then check the service itself. The directory does not tell you which SMA tests or treatments each hospital offers.

Ask whether the first visit is an assessment clinic, a general outpatient appointment or a procedure appointment. Confirm the registration fee separately from the consultation where possible, and ask what documents are required. If another person makes the call for the family, give them a short list of administrative questions. They do not need to send the complete medical folder to establish clinic days and referral requirements.

source.title: Federal Ministry of Health: teaching hospitals

sections.title: An example of a hospital to ask about
paragraphs: Memfys Hospital in Enugu, for example, describes a neurology unit and neurological diagnostic services on its website. You could discuss it with your referring doctor. Before making a journey, ask the hospital whether it assesses the person’s age group and concern, and where any necessary testing would be done.

Ask the hospital to confirm whether its relevant team can assess the specific concern and age group, what referral is needed and where any testing would be performed. Apply the same checks to a teaching hospital or another private service rather than inferring SMA capability from the word “neurology”.

sections.title: What the referral needs to explain
paragraphs: Ask the referring clinician to state what the receiving team is being asked to do: assess suspected neuromuscular weakness, interpret a confirmed genetic result, address a respiratory concern or provide another defined service. “Please see neurology” may be less helpful than a referral that explains the actual question and the person’s age group.

Keep the referral and complete supporting reports together. The receiving office should confirm how documents are submitted and whether they are needed before booking. If the family is travelling from another state, ask whether an administrative check can establish that the referral has reached the right department before the journey. That check does not replace the clinical appointment.

If a hospital cannot provide what is needed, take that answer back to the referring doctor and ask about another service. Keep the date and the name of the department you spoke to. There is a difference between finding a hospital number, booking an assessment and being accepted for a treatment; ask which has actually happened.

source.title: Federal Ministry of Health: teaching hospitals directory

sections.title: Questions to ask a hospital about SMA care
paragraphs: You could say: “We have a referral for suspected or confirmed SMA. Does your clinic assess this condition for a child or adult of this age? What documents do you need, how do we book, and what costs should we confirm before travelling?” Write down the response, the department, and the date.

If the person answering cannot confirm the service, ask which department can. Avoid relying solely on an old social-media post or a third-party directory. Confirm clinic days and referral arrangements again shortly before a long journey.

sections.title: Which professionals belong in the care team?
paragraphs: Ask the clinician which assessments are priorities now and which can be planned later. SMA Europe describes a multidisciplinary approach that may include neuromuscular, respiratory, rehabilitation, nutrition, and psychological expertise. The individual plan should determine the sequence rather than a family trying to book every possible specialist at once.

Neurology may coordinate diagnosis and treatment discussions. Respiratory professionals assess breathing-related needs; nutrition and swallowing professionals address feeding concerns; physiotherapy and occupational therapy can help with movement, positioning, equipment and participation. Psychological and social support can help the household navigate the pressures around care. Which roles are needed, and how urgently, depends on the individual assessment.

Ask why each appointment is needed. Is someone checking a breathing concern, helping with a school activity or teaching you to use equipment? Knowing the purpose makes it easier to prepare and to follow up if the appointment never arrives. You do not need to book every possible specialist at once.

source.title: Cure SMA: care standards and resources

sections.title: Coordinate SMA appointments and reports
paragraphs: Use one page with columns for clinician or service, role, next action, appointment date, contact route, and unresolved question. Keep the latest version with your medical folder. If advice appears inconsistent, ask the clinicians to clarify it; do not choose between conflicting instructions on your own.

A shared handover can be brief: current diagnosis, key reports, current care arrangements, the question for the receiving team and the contact responsible for follow-up. The clinician should confirm the clinical information. The family can add practical constraints such as travel from another state or the need to coordinate several visits. Keep the full reports available even when a short summary is used to introduce the case.

sections.title: What to do when a service or referral is delayed
paragraphs: If a service is unavailable, ask the referring clinician for an alternative route and what to do while waiting. Explain transport, cost, or accommodation constraints early. Ask whether administrative questions or report reviews can be handled remotely when clinically appropriate.

Before leaving any clinic, check that you know the next action and who will arrange it. If a call is promised, record when to follow up. Keep clinical contacts separate from accounts and booking contacts so you know where to direct each question. This small amount of organisation can make a complicated care journey easier to navigate.

If two instructions conflict, write down the difference and ask the teams to clarify it. If a service cannot be arranged, tell the clinician who recommended it. Ask what to do while waiting and which changes need urgent attention. They need to know when cost, travel or availability prevents the plan from happening.

sections.title: Keep a record of whom you have contacted
paragraphs: Use an official hospital contact and record the department, date and answer. A clinic’s name on an old post is not enough to establish what it offers today. Ask whether it assesses the person’s age group and whether a referral is required.

If an institution cannot confirm a service, mark it unconfirmed rather than treating silence as a booking. Ask the referring clinician about an alternative route. Do not use a mental-health or general “neuro” label as proof of neuromuscular expertise.

sections.title: How could a testing partnership change the route?
paragraphs: A laboratory partnership could make testing easier to arrange, but it needs more than a contact abroad. Families need doctors who can request the right test, reliable collection and shipping, clear fees and someone to explain the report. Those arrangements have to work together before the service can be offered.

SMA Hope is exploring possibilities, including international laboratory discussions. Until terms and operational arrangements are confirmed, this guide does not advertise a CENTOGENE partnership, a participating Nigerian centre or a subsidised test price.

For a family, a partnership needs to answer practical questions: who orders the test, where the sample is collected, which laboratory analyses it and who explains the result. The fees and arrangements for a failed sample matter too. Until those details are agreed, families should not rely on a partnership announcement as a way to obtain testing.

sections.title: Who does what: doctor, laboratory and foundation
paragraphs: It helps to know who is doing each job. A doctor examines the person and requests investigations. A laboratory analyses the sample and writes the report. A collection centre may only arrange the sample. SMA Hope can help you prepare questions, but does not do the examination or laboratory analysis.

Ask who handles each stage of a proposed test: the order, consent, collection, shipping, analysis and explanation. If the laboratory has agreed to receive a sample but local collection is not arranged, that is still an unresolved job. Find out who can arrange it before treating the test as booked.

We are exploring ways to improve access. Any service we introduce will need clear ordering, collection, shipping and result arrangements before families can use it. For now, ask the responsible clinic or laboratory for written details. Contact with the foundation does not guarantee a test, treatment or funding.
